section_header: Why Tinnitus Is More Than Noise
education_text: Tinnitus often feels like it is only about the sound: the ringing, buzzing, hissing, pulsing, or other noise that will not seem to turn off. That sound is real, and it can be distressing. But the experience of tinnitus is also shaped by what is happening in your body, your mind, and your daily life. This section introduces that bigger picture so the rest of the app makes sense.

education_text: It is natural to focus on the sound first. When tinnitus feels loud or intrusive, it can seem like everything would be better if the sound simply disappeared. Sound matters, and sound therapy is still one of the core tools we will use. But tinnitus distress often grows when other parts of life get pulled into the cycle: poor sleep, stress, fear, frustration, avoidance, and feeling misunderstood. Looking at the whole picture gives you more places to make useful change.

education_text: If tinnitus were only a hearing issue, then adding more sound would solve the whole problem. Many people do benefit from hearing aids, background sound, or other sound therapy tools, but those tools may not fully address the emotional and lifestyle impact of tinnitus. That does not mean sound therapy doesn’t work. It means tinnitus is being influenced by more than one system. The goal is not to find one perfect fix. The goal is to learn which parts of the experience you can influence, then build a plan around those levers.

section_header: Body: hearing, sound, and the nervous system
education_text: The body side of tinnitus includes the physical and medical parts of tinnitus. This may include hearing loss, noise exposure, aging, medication effects, injury, jaw or neck factors, or changes in how the auditory system and nervous system respond to sound. Sound therapy and hearing care live here because they change what the ears and brain are receiving. If hearing loss is present, audiology care and appropriate amplification can be a major part of tinnitus management.

education_text: The mind side of tinnitus includes your reactions to tinnitus: attention, worry, fear, frustration, self-talk, and the meaning your brain attaches to the sound. This is not saying tinnitus is imaginary. The sound is real. The point is that your reaction to the sound can make it feel more threatening, more intrusive, or harder to live with. Skills like mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, acceptance, and self-compassion all work with this part of the tinnitus experience.

section_header: Life: sleep, routines, relationships, and the world around you
education_text: The life side of tinnitus includes the ways tinnitus changes your day-to-day routines and relationships. You might avoid quiet rooms, skip social events, struggle at work, feel misunderstood, or notice that sleep becomes more stressful. These are not small side issues. They are part of how tinnitus becomes dominant. Communication skills, sleep education, sound planning, and gradual re-engagement help you keep your life from shrinking around tinnitus.

section_header: Pause & Reflect: Why am I doing this?
education_text: Before you start learning tools, take a moment to name your reason for being here. Are you looking for relief, understanding, better sleep, more confidence, or a way to make everyday life feel easier? Then imagine six months from now. Naming your why can make the rest of the work feel more connected to your life.

section_header: Using helpful sounds to manage tinnitus
education_text:
Sound therapy means using comfortable outside sound to make tinnitus less dominant in your listening environment. The goal is not to blast tinnitus away or prove that you can ignore it. The goal is to give your ears and brain another sound to work with so tinnitus can gradually become less central.

This is often one of the most practical starting points in tinnitus management because it works directly with the sound experience. When sound therapy is used consistently and comfortably, it can help set the stage for the other skills in this app, including acceptance, mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, and sleep support.

section_header: What you will learn in this section
education_text:
By the end of this section, you should understand why sound therapy can help the brain get used to tinnitus, how to choose sounds and devices that feel comfortable, and how to set the volume so tinnitus and sound therapy gently overlap.

The most important skill is finding the right volume level. Sound that is too quiet will not help much, while sound that completely covers tinnitus may become a form of avoidance. The useful range is where the sound therapy is clearly present, but tinnitus is not being pushed out of awareness entirely.

education_text:
When tinnitus is the only noticeable sound, the brain may treat it as the most important thing in the room. Sound therapy changes that listening environment. By adding a neutral or soothing background sound, you reduce the contrast between silence and tinnitus.

Over time, this can help the brain treat tinnitus as a lower-priority signal. It may still be there, but it does not have to take center stage or pull your attention as strongly. This process is gradual, and it works best when sound therapy is used patiently and consistently.

education_text:
Sound therapy means adding soft, steady, or soothing sound to your environment. This might come from a fan, a sound machine, a phone app, a speaker, open-ear headphones, or hearing aids. The sound does not have to be special or complicated. It just needs to be comfortable and useful for you.

Think of sound therapy as an auditory backdrop. The outside sound gives your brain something else to hear, so tinnitus is not standing alone in silence. The aim is not to erase tinnitus in the moment, but to make the listening environment easier for your brain to handle.

education_text:
A simple way to understand sound therapy is to imagine sitting in a restaurant. Music, voices, and movement do not erase every small sound in the room, but they help those sounds blend into the background. The clink of silverware may still happen, but it usually does not demand your full attention.

Tinnitus can work in a similar way. When the room is completely quiet, tinnitus may feel isolated and intense. When gentle sound is added, tinnitus may still be present, but it has more competition and can begin to feel less intrusive.

section_header: Why silence can make tinnitus feel louder
education_text:
Many people notice tinnitus most strongly in quiet. That does not necessarily mean tinnitus has become more dangerous or permanently louder. It may mean there is less outside sound competing for attention.

Sound therapy reduces the stark contrast between silence and tinnitus. That can lower the feeling that tinnitus is the only thing happening. For some people this helps with concentration, relaxation, evening routines, and sleep preparation. It also gives the brain repeated opportunities to learn that tinnitus can be present without needing an alarm response.

section_header: Masking is not the same as sound therapy
education_text:
Many people use the word masking to mean any use of sound for tinnitus, but full masking and sound therapy are not the same thing. Full masking means turning sound up until tinnitus is completely covered. That can be useful for a short break or a high-distress moment, but it is not the main goal of sound therapy, as we discuss it here.

Sound therapy usually works best when it supports adaptation. That means the sound is comfortable and present, while tinnitus may still be partly audible. In that volume range, the brain can begin learning that tinnitus does not need to dominate or trigger constant monitoring.

education_text:
Full masking can feel good because it gives immediate relief from hearing tinnitus. The limitation is that the relief often stops when the masking sound stops. If the brain only learns that tinnitus must be hidden, tinnitus may feel more threatening when it returns.

A habituation-oriented sound therapy approach is different. It allows some awareness of tinnitus while adding a steady, supportive sound. This can help the brain learn that tinnitus is present but not urgent. That learning is usually slower than short-term masking, but it is often more useful for daily management.

section_header: Finding the sound therapy sweet spot
education_text:
The sound therapy sweet spot is the range where you can hear both the sound therapy and your tinnitus. If the sound therapy is too quiet, it may not give your brain enough input to work with. If it is too loud and completely covers tinnitus, it may become more about escaping the sound than adapting to it.

The middle volume range is usually the most helpful. In that range, tinnitus is present, but it is not alone. Sound therapy becomes a calm companion to your listening environment rather than a battle to overpower tinnitus.

education_text:
Habituation means the brain adapts and becomes less reactive to a repeated stimulus. When habituation happens with tinnitus, you may still notice tinnitus if you listen for it, but it no longer creates the same stress or urgency.

Sound therapy means using gentle background sound to reduce the impact of tinnitus and support habituation. An external sound source is any device or method that delivers that sound, such as a fan, speaker, phone app, sound machine, hearing aids, or open-ear headphones.

education_text:
There is no perfect sound for everyone. Some people like rain, ocean waves, crickets, fans, white noise, pink noise, gentle music, or other steady sounds. Some people like sounds that another person would find irritating. If it helps you and you can use it comfortably, it can be a good sound for you.

The best starting point is to try a few neutral or pleasant sounds and notice which ones feel comfortable or soothing. If a sound becomes annoying, you are not doing anything wrong. Try a different sound or change the setting.

Start with the sound low. Slowly raise it until you can hear the sound therapy clearly. Then notice whether tinnitus is still partly present. If you cannot hear the sound therapy, it is too low. If tinnitus disappears completely, the sound may be louder than you need for everyday sound therapy.

Aim for a comfortable overlap. You should be aware of the support sound, and you may still notice tinnitus, but neither one should feel like it is taking over. The exact level may change from day to day, and that is okay.

section_header: Using sound therapy during the day
education_text:
Sound therapy is often most useful during quiet tasks or times when tinnitus tends to grab your attention. You might use it while reading, doing work around the home, working at a desk, relaxing in the evening, or preparing for bed.

Consistency matters more than perfection. You do not need to analyze every minute. The goal is to give your brain repeated, comfortable exposure to a richer sound environment so tinnitus becomes less dominant over time.

education_text:
Many people notice tinnitus more at night because the environment is quieter and there are fewer distractions. Gentle sound at night can make the transition toward sleep feel less like a direct confrontation with tinnitus.

This does not mean sound therapy is a full sleep treatment. It is one supportive tool. If sleep is a persistent problem, or if there are signs of a sleep condition such as sleep apnea, that deserves proper evaluation. But for many people, a comfortable background sound can make bedtime feel less stark and less silent.

Tinnitus and sound sensitivity often travel together. If ordinary sound feels sharp, uncomfortable, or threatening, it can be tempting to avoid sound as much as possible. That reaction makes sense, but living in a quieter and quieter world can sometimes keep the sound system on high alert.

For sound sensitivity, the same basic principle still applies: comfortable, controlled sound can help the system feel safer over time. The key is not to push into volume levels that are uncomfortable or painful. Start gently, stay below the point of sensitivity, and use sounds that feel enjoyable or neutral.

education_text:
One simple sound-sensitivity practice is to use enjoyable music on speakers for 10 to 15 minutes. Start with the volume all the way down. Slowly raise it until you begin to notice sensitivity, then lower it slightly below that point. Listen only if it feels comfortable.

The purpose is not to tolerate bothersome sound levels. The purpose is to give your brain and body a controlled sound experience where nothing bad happens. If the level changes from day to day, treat that information non-judgmentally.

section_header: FAQ: How loud should sound therapy be?
education_text:
A useful starting point is just below the level where sound therapy would completely cover tinnitus. You want to hear the support sound and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap is what makes it sound therapy rather than simply blocking tinnitus out.

There may be moments when fuller masking is useful for a short break. For daily management, though, the balanced volume level is usually the better target.

section_header: FAQ: Does the type of sound matter?
education_text:
The type of sound matters mostly because you need to be able to use it comfortably. Nature sounds, steady noise, fan sounds, gentle music, crickets, or water sounds can all be reasonable options.

The best sound is not the one someone else calls perfect. It is the one that works for your ears, your environment, and your nervous system on that day.

section_header: Acceptance and change can work together
education_text:
When tinnitus feels difficult, it is natural to want it gone. That reaction makes sense. The problem is that tinnitus does not always respond to force, and the harder you fight to make it disappear in a single moment, the more your attention and energy can become wrapped around it.

Acceptance does not mean giving up. In this section, acceptance means acknowledging what is happening right now so you can use your energy more wisely. Change means taking practical steps that reduce distress, support daily life, and help you stay connected to what matters.

section_header: Acceptance means noticing what is here
education_text:
Acceptance means allowing yourself to notice that tinnitus is present without spending all your energy trying to erase it. It does not mean you like tinnitus. It does not mean you want it to stay. It does not mean you believe nothing can improve.

It means you are starting from reality: tinnitus is here right now, and the next useful step probably will not come from arguing with that fact.

section_header: Change means acting where you have influence
education_text:
Change means taking active steps to improve your life and reduce distress. That might mean using sound therapy, asking for support, practicing mindfulness, communicating a need, or returning to an activity tinnitus has pushed aside.

Change does not have to mean forcing tinnitus to disappear. It can mean making today more workable, your environment more supportive, and your reactions less controlled by the sound.

section_header: Why trying only to eliminate tinnitus can backfire
education_text:
At the beginning, many people put all their energy into making tinnitus vanish. They may avoid quiet places, stop doing things they enjoy, search constantly for cures, or feel crushed whenever a treatment does not work right away.

Those reactions are understandable. But when your whole life becomes organized around eliminating tinnitus, tinnitus can become even more central. The struggle itself starts taking up the space that your routines, relationships, hobbies, and rest used to occupy.

Over time, the world may get smaller. Acceptance helps reverse that pattern by asking, “What can I allow for this moment, and what useful action can I take anyway?”

section_header: Sound therapy shows acceptance and change together
education_text:
Sound therapy is a good example of acceptance and change working together. If you use sound only to cover tinnitus completely all day, the purpose becomes escape. That may help briefly, but it can also keep the brain from learning that tinnitus is safe enough to tune out.

When sound therapy is set in the middle volume range, where you can hear the support sound and may still notice tinnitus, you are accepting enough of the sound for the brain to learn while still changing the environment to make it easier to tolerate.

The Yes AND mindset comes from the idea that two truths can exist at the same time. You can acknowledge tinnitus honestly and still take a useful next step.

For example: “Yes, my tinnitus is tough today, and I can use a gentle background sound while I get ready.” Or, “Yes, I wish this were different, and I can still go to dinner with friends.” The first half is acceptance. The second half is change.

A more balanced view says: tinnitus can be present, and I can still take care of myself. I can dislike this sound, and I can still choose something meaningful. I can want improvement, and I can stop demanding that everything change before I live my life.

education_text:
Imagine tinnitus on the other side of a rope in a tug of war. You pull harder and harder, trying to win. But the more you pull, the more tired and stuck you become.

The question is not whether those reactions make sense. They do, and are reasonable things to do at first. The question is whether staying in the tug-of-war is giving you your life back.

Silence is not required. Everyday sounds can become anchors for awareness.

If you notice tinnitus, label it neutrally as “ringing,” then gently widen attention to the rest of the sound environment.

Continue moving back and forth in short intervals.

section_header: Why panic makes tinnitus feel bigger
education_text: When you feel panicked about tinnitus, your brain pays closer attention to the sound. That extra attention can make tinnitus feel louder, sharper, or more threatening, even if the signal itself has not changed much. Distress tolerance interrupts this loop. A cold splash of water, a pause, a breath, or a short movement break gives your body another high-priority signal and gives your mind a chance to stop chasing the alarm.

section_header: Use the word fluctuation, not spike
education_text: Language matters. The word spike can make a tinnitus change sound like a permanent emergency. The word fluctuation is more neutral. It reminds you that tinnitus can move up and down, shift in tone, and feel more or less intrusive depending on the day, the body, stress, sleep, attention, and environment. A difficult fluctuation can still be unpleasant, but naming it as a fluctuation helps reduce the automatic fear that it will stay this way forever.

The goal is safe, noticeable body-based regulation.

section_header: How distress tolerance connects to the bigger picture
education_text: Distress tolerance sits between mindfulness and cognitive reframing. Mindfulness helps you notice what is happening. Distress tolerance helps when the intensity is too high to think clearly. Once the tornado slows down, cognitive reframing can help you look at the thoughts that made the moment feel even worse. This section also connects to acceptance: even if you cannot change tinnitus right now, you can change how you respond to the moment.

section_header: Cognitive Reframing: Challenging Negative Thought Patterns
education_text: When tinnitus or sound sensitivity feels intense, the mind can jump quickly to conclusions: “This will ruin my whole day,” “I cannot handle any noise,” or “Nothing will ever get better.” Cognitive reframing helps you slow that process down. The goal is not to pretend tinnitus is easy or to force positive thinking. The goal is to notice the thought, check whether it is accurate, and build a more balanced response.

section_header: What You’ll Learn in This Section
education_text: In this section, you will learn how to spot recurring tinnitus-related thought patterns, test distressing thoughts with evidence, and reframe them into statements that are more accurate and workable. You will also see how these skills can apply beyond tinnitus, including work stress, relationships, sleep concerns, and other moments when the mind jumps to worst-case conclusions.

section_header: Why Tinnitus Thoughts Can Move So Fast
education_text: When tinnitus flares or sound sensitivity is triggered, your thoughts may move faster than your ability to evaluate them. A sound moment can become a story: “This is unbearable,” “I am powerless,” or “My day is over.” Those thoughts can increase anxiety or hopelessness, which can then lead to avoidance, checking, withdrawal, or frantic searching for relief. The sound may be real, but the story your mind adds can make the distress much larger.

section_header: The Thoughts, Feelings, and Behaviors Loop
education_text: Cognitive behavioral therapy often describes a loop between what we think, how we feel, and what we do. With tinnitus, the loop might start with noticing the sound. That leads to a thought such as, “Today is going to be terrible.” That thought creates dread, and the dread may lead you to cancel plans, check tinnitus repeatedly, or search for a quick fix. Those behaviors then reinforce the next thought. Reframing gives you an off-ramp in that loop.

Those behaviors then reinforce the next thought. Reframing gives you an off-ramp in that loop.

education_text: Think of cognitive restructuring as reality-checking your mind. First, identify the distressing thought. Next, ask whether the thought is fully accurate or whether it is leaving out evidence. Then create a more balanced statement. For example, “This ringing is awful, so my day is ruined” might become, “This moment is difficult, and I have had difficult tinnitus moments before without the entire day being lost.”

section_header: Pause and Look Back on a Quick Reaction
education_text: A helpful way to understand reframing is to remember a time when you reacted quickly, then later saw the situation differently. Think of a recent tinnitus moment when your reaction was immediate. How did it feel then? How does it feel now? Were your fears still fully accurate later? This kind of reflection shows that the first thought is not always the most complete thought.

education_text: Cognitive restructuring is not about telling yourself that tinnitus is wonderful or that everything is fine. That would not be honest, and for many people it would not be believable. The goal is accuracy. “I will never have a good moment again” is usually too extreme. “Some days are hard, and I have also had moments where tinnitus bothered me less” is more balanced. That balance reduces the extra distress created by the thought.

section_header: Why Reframing Helps Even If the Sound Is Still There
education_text: Cognitive reframing may not change the tinnitus itself. Instead, it changes the stress loop around the sound. When the mind treats tinnitus as danger, failure, or a permanent disaster, distress grows. When the mind learns to test those meanings, the emotional reaction often becomes more manageable. Tinnitus can still be unpleasant, but it does not have to control every next step.

education_text: The same pattern can happen with sound sensitivity. A sound may feel uncomfortable, and the mind may quickly jump to “I cannot handle any noise” or “I have to avoid everything.” Sometimes caution is appropriate, especially around painful or unsafe sound. But reframing helps you separate reasonable protection from a story that makes life smaller than it needs to be.

You may have had loud tinnitus before and still had a meaningful, productive, or even good day. A more balanced statement might be, “This morning is difficult, and I can use my tools while I see how the day unfolds.”

education_text: Cognitive reframing works best when it is practiced in real life. Start with a small moment: “I will never get through this meeting,” “This sound is too much,” or “I am failing at tinnitus management.” Write the thought down, check the facts, and create a more balanced statement. Over time, the skill becomes less like a worksheet and more like a mental pause you can use in the moment.

section_header: You Will Miss Most Thoughts at First
education_text: At the beginning, you may miss most automatic thoughts until after the moment has passed. That is normal. The first goal is not to catch every thought. The goal is to notice one pattern that you would have missed before. If you catch one out of twenty, that is progress, because the pattern is becoming visible.

education_text: Cognitive distortions are common thinking shortcuts. They are not signs that you are doing something wrong; they are patterns to notice. Naming the pattern gives you a little distance from it. You do not need to pick the perfect label. If the label helps you pause and question the thought, it has done its job.

education_text: All-or-nothing thinking turns a complicated situation into two choices: perfect or ruined. With tinnitus, this might sound like, “If my tinnitus does not go away completely, my life will be ruined.” A more balanced view looks for the middle ground: life may be harder right now, and it can still contain useful, meaningful, or manageable moments.

education_text: Overgeneralization takes one moment and stretches it too far. “My tinnitus was loud today, so it will be like this every day” is a prediction based on limited evidence. Reframing asks what else you know from experience: tinnitus often changes, and one day does not prove the future.

education_text: Filtering means the mind locks onto the distressing evidence and filters out everything else. You might dismiss a good day because today is harder. Reframing does not deny today’s difficulty; it asks you to include the fuller picture.

education_text: Mind reading happens when you assume you know what others think. With tinnitus, it may sound like, “People think I am overreacting.” Sometimes people may not understand, but that is different from knowing what they think. Reframing asks what evidence you actually have and whether communication could help.

education_text: Minimizing downplays progress. If you used sound therapy, practiced breathing, went to dinner, or had a quieter hour, that matters. The improvement may not be perfect, but it is still evidence that your choices can influence the experience.

education_text: Catastrophizing turns a hard moment into a disaster story. “My tinnitus will only get worse, and I will never handle it” may feel convincing when distress is high. Reframing asks whether the evidence truly proves that outcome, and what a more grounded next thought could be.

education_text: Control fallacies make it feel like you have either total control or no control at all. Tinnitus management usually lives in the middle. You may not control every sound moment, but you can influence your sound environment, attention, routines, and response.

education_text: Labeling turns a struggle into an identity. “I am having a hard tinnitus day” is very different from “I am a failure.” Reframing helps separate the difficulty of the moment from your worth as a person.

education_text: No. Forced positivity would ask you to say something cheerful that you do not believe. Cognitive restructuring asks whether the thought is accurate, complete, and useful. You still acknowledge discomfort, but you do not let worst-case assumptions become the only story.

section_header: DEAR MAN: a structure for clear requests
education_text: DEAR MAN is a DBT communication tool for making a request or saying no clearly. The first part, DEAR, helps you organize what you want to say: describe the situation, express how it affects you, assert what you need, and reinforce why the request helps. The second part, MAN, helps you stay focused, appear confident, and negotiate when needed.

education_text: Start with the facts. Describe the situation in neutral terms: “The TV volume is making it hard for me to stay comfortable.” Then express how it affects you: “I feel overwhelmed when it stays this loud.” Next, assert the request clearly: “Could we lower it a little?” Finally, reinforce why it helps: “That would let me stay in the room and enjoy the evening with you.”

Negotiating means staying open to workable solutions, such as moving seats, lowering volume, or taking a short break.

section_header: Why sleep belongs in tinnitus management
education_text: Sleep may seem separate from tinnitus, but the two are often closely connected. When sleep is poor, your stress system has less time to recover, your attention may narrow, and difficult sounds can feel harder to ignore. When tinnitus feels threatening at bedtime, sleep can become harder to reach. That is why sleep belongs in a multimodal tinnitus plan.

education_text: A difficult night can lead to fatigue, irritability, and more worry the next day. That stress can make tinnitus feel more intrusive, especially when you are tired. Then, when bedtime returns, the memory of the previous bad night can make you anxious before you even lie down. This loop can feel powerful, but it also gives you several places to intervene.

section_header: Why quiet nights can feel harder
education_text: Tinnitus often stands out when the environment becomes quiet. At night, there may be fewer external sounds, fewer tasks, and less social distraction. The brain can begin scanning for the ringing, buzzing, or hissing, and that attention can make the sound feel more important. This is one reason soft, steady background sound can be helpful at bedtime.

section_header: Why trying harder to sleep can backfire
education_text: Sleep is unusual because effort does not always help. Trying to force sleep can make your mind more alert, especially if you start checking the clock, measuring the night, or predicting how bad tomorrow will be. The goal is not to work harder at sleeping. The goal is to create conditions where sleep is more likely to happen naturally.

section_header: Sleep drive: your body’s pressure for sleep
education_text: Sleep drive is the natural pressure for sleep that builds the longer you are awake. When people spend too much time in bed awake, nap excessively, or go to bed much earlier to make up for a poor night, that pressure can weaken. A stronger sleep drive can make sleep more continuous and less fragile.

section_header: When the bed becomes a place for frustration
education_text: If you lie awake night after night, the bed can start to feel connected with frustration, worry, clock-checking, and tinnitus monitoring. Your brain may learn that bed means wakefulness instead of sleep. Stimulus control is a behavioral sleep idea designed to rebuild the connection between bed and successful sleep.

education_text: In sleep treatment, stimulus control often means going to bed when sleepy, leaving bed if you are awake for a while, doing something quiet and relaxing, and returning when sleepiness returns. The point is not punishment, and it is not a test of willpower. It is a way of helping the brain relearn that bed is for sleep, not for hours of struggling.

education_text: Sleep-related thoughts can become convincing at night. These thoughts may feel true in the moment, but they can often be checked and softened.

Thoughts like “If I do not sleep eight hours, tomorrow is ruined” or “I will never fall asleep with tinnitus” can raise anxiety and make the body more alert. These thoughts may feel true in the moment, but they can often be checked and softened.

education_text: Sleep myths create pressure. You may hear that everyone needs exactly eight hours, that one bad night ruins the next day, or that staying in bed awake will eventually force sleep. A more balanced view is usually more helpful: sleep needs vary, bad nights happen, and your body can often function better than your anxious mind predicts.

education_text: Examples of sleep myths include: “I must get eight hours or I will fail,” “I can always catch up on weekends,” “alcohol helps me sleep better,” “complete silence is best,” “if I stay in bed long enough I will force sleep,” and “more time in bed always means more rest.” Each of these has a more balanced version that lowers pressure.

education_text: Sound can help at night by reducing the contrast between silence and tinnitus. The sound should usually be low-level, steady, and comfortable. Loud, surprising, or highly varied sound may keep the brain more alert. The goal is not to create a perfect sound environment. The goal is to make the night feel less stark and less tinnitus-focused.

section_header: Sleep hygiene is helpful, but it is not the whole answer
education_text: Sleep hygiene includes habits that support sleep: a consistent schedule, a calmer wind-down, less late caffeine, a comfortable bedroom, and fewer stimulating activities right before bed. These habits matter, but sleep hygiene alone may not fix insomnia. For many people, the bigger shift comes from changing the thoughts and behaviors that keep the bed connected with stress.

education_text: A consistent sleep schedule helps your body clock predict when sleep and wakefulness should happen. A regular wake time is especially important, even after a rough night. This does not mean you must be rigid forever. It means giving your body repeated cues so the sleep system has a clearer rhythm.

education_text: A wind-down routine gives the brain a transition. Reading, gentle stretching, quiet breathing, or calming audio can help signal that the day is ending. Try to avoid stressful work, intense conversations, or stimulating tasks right before bed when possible. The purpose is not to force sleep, but to lower the activation level around bedtime.

education_text: A bedroom that is cool, dark, comfortable, and low in disruption can make sleep easier. For tinnitus, “quiet” does not always mean silent. A soft, steady sound can be useful if silence makes tinnitus stand out. Try to keep the bed connected mainly with sleep, so your brain has a clear signal about what the space is for.

education_text: Caffeine and nicotine can make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, especially later in the day. Alcohol may feel relaxing at first, but it can fragment sleep later in the night. Heavy meals close to bedtime can be disruptive for some people. Regular movement can support sleep, while intense late workouts may be too activating for some.

education_text: If worries or to-do lists flood in at night, try giving them another place to go earlier in the evening. Some people write down worries, next steps, or tomorrow’s tasks before the wind-down begins. Breathing, mindfulness, or paired muscle relaxation can also help the body shift out of problem-solving mode.

education_text: Stimulus control is the idea of rebuilding the connection between bed and sleep. Sleep drive is the pressure for sleep that builds while you are awake. Sleep distortions are rigid or threatening thoughts about sleep. Sleep hygiene is the set of habits and environmental choices that support healthier sleep.

section_header: CBT-I and brief behavioral sleep care
education_text: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia, often called CBT-I, is a structured treatment for insomnia. Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia, or BBTI, is a shorter behavioral approach. This app does not provide either treatment. It introduces a few ideas that can help you understand your options and decide whether professional sleep support may be worth exploring. These programs can be good starting points to search for, if you need more help.

section_header: FAQ: Should I stay in bed and force sleep?
education_text: Usually, forcing sleep makes things harder. Lying awake for long stretches can teach the brain that bed is a place for wakefulness and frustration. A calmer approach is to reduce the struggle, do something quiet if needed, and return when sleepiness comes back.

section_header: FAQ: Why am I still awake if I already use sleep hygiene?
education_text: Sleep hygiene is useful, but it is not always enough. If the main problem is worry, clock-checking, long periods awake in bed, or fear of tinnitus at night, then thought patterns and bedtime behaviors may need attention too.

education_text: TV or phone audio may feel helpful at first, but it can also be stimulating, bright, varied, or attention-grabbing. If you use sound at night, aim for soft, steady, neutral sound that supports rest rather than pulling your attention back into the screen or the story.
